meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 1: MCP Fundamentals
meta.revision: v2.1 (curated 2026-09-12, 200 items, verified against the 2026-07-28 specification)

questions.question: Your company runs 5 AI applications that each need access to the same 8 internal systems. What does adopting MCP change about the number of integrations you build and maintain?

options.text: 40 bespoke connectors become 13 implementations: one client per app, one server per system
The count is unchanged, but each connector becomes smaller because MCP handles transport
40 bespoke connectors become 8, because each app reuses the same connector code
40 bespoke connectors become 5, because one server can front all 8 systems

questions.explanation: MCP turns an M x N integration problem into M + N: each application ships one MCP client, each system one MCP server, and any client can talk to any server. Reusing connector code (B) or fronting several systems behind one server (D) are implementation choices, not what the protocol changes.

questions.question: Which existing standard is MCP explicitly modelled on, and what is the parallel?

options.text: OpenAPI: one description format replaces hand-written API client libraries
GraphQL: one query endpoint replaces many resource-specific REST endpoints
OAuth 2.1: one authorization framework replaces per-service credential schemes
Language Server Protocol: one protocol replaces per-editor, per-language plugins

questions.explanation: The specification says MCP takes inspiration from the Language Server Protocol, which standardized how language support is added across the whole ecosystem of development tools. MCP does use OAuth 2.1 for HTTP authorization, but that is one component, not the protocol's model.

questions.question: Your team maintains an internal ticketing API and wants Claude Desktop users to reach it. Which MCP participant do you implement?

options.text: A server, which exposes the ticketing API through tools, resources or prompts
A host, because the host is what holds the connection to external systems
Both a client and a server, since every MCP connection needs one of each end
A client, because the client is the component that connects out to an API

questions.explanation: Servers expose capabilities; hosts (the AI application) create clients that connect to them. Claude Desktop already provides the host and the client, so you only write the server.

questions.question: Which set correctly lists what a server may offer versus what a client may offer?

options.text: Server: tools, elicitation, sampling. Client: resources and prompts
Server: resources, prompts, tools. Client: elicitation
Server: tools and prompts. Client: resources, roots and logging
Server: resources and tools. Client: prompts and elicitation

questions.explanation: Servers offer resources, prompts and tools. In 2026-07-28 the only active client feature is elicitation; sampling and roots still exist but are deprecated, and logging is a server utility.

questions.question: A server ships a '/incident-review' prompt template. In MCP's control model, who decides when it gets used, and who decides what it contains?

options.text: The user chooses when to invoke it; the server authors its content
The user chooses when to invoke it and the host rewrites its content for the model
The host chooses when to invoke it based on conversation heuristics; the user edits it
The model chooses when to invoke it; the server authors its content

questions.explanation: Prompts are user-controlled: they are exposed so the user can explicitly select them, typically as slash commands. That refers to who decides when a prompt is used, not who writes it; prompt content is defined by the server.

questions.question: You ship one server over stdio for local use and the same server over Streamable HTTP for your team. What does the specification say about authorization for the two deployments?

options.text: No: it is optional everywhere, and stdio servers may use OAuth if they prefer
No: it is optional, HTTP transports SHOULD conform, and stdio SHOULD NOT use it
Yes for servers that expose tools, no for servers that expose only resources
Yes: every server must implement OAuth 2.1 regardless of transport

questions.explanation: Authorization is OPTIONAL. Implementations using HTTP-based transports SHOULD conform to the authorization spec; implementations using stdio SHOULD NOT, and instead retrieve credentials from the environment.

questions.question: A server author asks which endpoint they should call to run the model once their tool has gathered its data. What do you tell them?

options.text: Servers call the host's completion endpoint, which proxies the request to the model
Servers request inference through sampling, which every host is required to support
Servers do not call a model at all; the host runs inference and uses the result
Servers call the model directly using the credentials passed in the request _meta

questions.explanation: MCP gives a model access to context; it does not give servers access to a model. The host owns the model and the conversation. Sampling, which once let servers ask for a completion, is deprecated in 2026-07-28 and was never mandatory.

questions.question: Your host wants to attach the user's calendar, read from one server, as context for a request going to a different server. What does the consent principle require?

options.text: Nothing extra, provided the receiving server declares a privacy policy in server/discover
Nothing extra, because both servers were installed by the same user in the same host
A signed data-sharing assertion from the first server, verified by the second server
Explicit user consent before user data is exposed to that server, obtained by the host

questions.explanation: Hosts must obtain explicit user consent before exposing user data to any server, and must not pass data around between servers without it. The user installing a server is consent to connect, not consent to hand it everything.

questions.question: A teammate says 'our service is MCP-compatible: we expose JSON over REST webhooks and the model calls them'. Why does that not make it an MCP server?

options.text: MCP requires every server to be published in the official MCP Registry first
MCP requires servers to be built with one of the official SDKs, in one of the languages it supports
MCP requires JSON-RPC 2.0 messages over a defined transport, not arbitrary REST endpoints
MCP requires OAuth 2.1, which webhook endpoints cannot provide

questions.explanation: All MCP messages MUST follow JSON-RPC 2.0 and travel over a defined transport (stdio or Streamable HTTP). SDKs and registry publication are optional, and authorization itself is optional (stdio servers take credentials from the environment).

questions.question: Which three capabilities does the specification say MCP provides a standardized way to do?

options.text: Cache prompts, route requests between providers, and meter token consumption per user
Share context with models, expose tools and capabilities, build composable integrations
Authenticate users, encrypt traffic in transit, and audit every action a model takes
Fine-tune models, evaluate their output, and serve inference behind a single API

questions.explanation: The overview lists exactly these three: sharing contextual information with language models, exposing tools and capabilities to AI systems, and building composable integrations and workflows. Model training, inference routing and metering are outside MCP's scope.

questions.question: MCP protocol versions look like 2026-07-28. What does that date actually mean?

options.text: The earliest date on which implementations must stop supporting older revisions
The last date on which backwards-incompatible changes were made to the protocol
The date the revision was first published as a draft for community review
The date the specification repository cut its most recent release tag

questions.explanation: A version string is the date of the last backwards-incompatible change, not a release or deprecation date. Backwards-compatible changes can land without changing the version string.

questions.question: Who stewards MCP today, and under what legal entity?

options.text: The OpenJS Foundation, which also hosts the official SDKs and the public registry
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation, which took over the project from Anthropic
The Agentic AI Foundation at the Linux Foundation, as a Series of LF Projects, LLC
Anthropic, which retains ownership and publishes the specification under its own terms

questions.explanation: Anthropic created and announced MCP in November 2024 and contributed it to the Agentic AI Foundation when the AAIF launched in December 2025. The project runs as a Series of LF Projects, LLC.

questions.question: A host auto-approves every tool call from servers the user installed, arguing that installation was consent. Which specification principle does that violate?

options.text: User consent and control: users must be able to revoke a server at any time
None: pre-approval of an installed server's tools is explicitly permitted
Tool safety: hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool
Data privacy: resource data must not leave the host without consent

questions.explanation: Tools represent arbitrary code execution, so hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool and users should understand what each tool does. Blanket approval at install time is not the consent the spec means, though hosts may offer per-tool pre-approval UI.

questions.question: A tool definition carries an annotation claiming it is read-only. How should a client treat that claim?

options.text: As authoritative for display, but it must still be re-checked after execution
As untrusted metadata, unless the server itself is trusted
As a hint the host must show to the user but may not act on in any way
As authoritative, because annotations are validated by the protocol schema

questions.explanation: Descriptions of tool behaviour, including annotations, must be considered untrusted unless they come from a trusted server. A malicious server can label a destructive tool read-only.

questions.question: In 2026-07-28, what does 'MCP is a stateless protocol' mean in practice for a single request?

options.text: Servers must reconstruct prior conversation turns from the client's message history
All information needed to process it is in the request, including version and capabilities
Each request opens a fresh connection, which is closed again as soon as the result is sent back
Servers may not store any data between calls, so tools cannot have side effects

questions.explanation: Statelessness is about the protocol session, not about storage: every request carries its own protocol version and capabilities in _meta, and a server must not infer context from earlier requests on the same connection. Servers can still hold application state, referenced by explicit handles.

questions.question: You are wrapping a public cloud API that many users will reach from different machines. Which transport fits, and why?

options.text: stdio: it avoids network exposure and is the recommended default for all servers
Either one: transports are interchangeable because the data layer is identical
HTTP+SSE: it is the two-endpoint transport designed for multi-tenant servers
Streamable HTTP: one deployment serves many clients and supports OAuth

questions.explanation: stdio is for local, same-machine servers launched as a subprocess. HTTP+SSE has been deprecated since 2025-03-26. Streamable HTTP is the remote transport, and it is where the MCP authorization framework applies.

questions.question: A server author asks for the full chat transcript so their tool can 'understand context'. What does MCP's design say?

options.text: Servers receive only necessary context; the full conversation stays with the host
Servers get the transcript whenever the user has approved the server at install time
Servers can read it via resources/read on a host-provided conversation resource
Servers may request the transcript through sampling, which the host must satisfy

questions.explanation: A core design principle is that servers should not be able to read the whole conversation nor see into other servers. Each server receives only the contextual information it needs, and the host enforces that boundary.

questions.question: Your server can expose a customer record two ways: as something the model calls whenever it decides it needs data, or as context the host attaches to the conversation. Which primitives are those, in that order?

options.text: A prompt, which is model-controlled; and a resource, which is user-controlled
A resource, which is model-controlled; and a tool, which is application-controlled
A tool, which is model-controlled; and a prompt, which is application-controlled
A tool, which is model-controlled; and a resource, which is application-controlled

questions.explanation: Tools are model-controlled: the model decides when to invoke them. Resources are application-controlled: the host decides what to attach. Prompts are user-controlled, surfaced as an explicit choice such as a slash command.

questions.question: You are writing a client for 2026-07-28 and must decide what goes in the _meta of every single request. Which fields are REQUIRED there?

options.text: protocolVersion only, since capabilities are negotiated once per connection
clientCapabilities and a progressToken, with protocolVersion in a header only
protocolVersion and clientCapabilities, on every request
protocolVersion and clientInfo, with clientCapabilities optional

questions.explanation: Because there is no handshake, each request carries its own context: protocolVersion and clientCapabilities are REQUIRED in _meta, clientInfo SHOULD be present, and logLevel and progressToken are optional. Nothing is negotiated once per connection any more.

questions.question: Your host is about to invoke a tool whose description says it deletes records. What does the specification expect of the host at that moment?

options.text: Show the user what will run and get approval, because tool results drive real-world effects
Run it and log the call, since the user consented when they installed the server
Refuse the call outright, because destructive operations are not permitted over MCP
Run it only if the tool omits a destructiveHint annotation, which signals a safe operation

questions.explanation: The specification requires hosts to obtain explicit user consent before invoking tools and to show the user what is about to happen. Installation is not blanket consent, annotations are untrusted hints, and MCP does not forbid destructive tools.

questions.question: A colleague claims an MCP server can pop a question to the user whenever it likes, the way a desktop app shows a notification. Why is that wrong?

options.text: A server can only ask while handling a request, and the client may still decline or cancel
A server can ask at any time, but only through the host's logging channel
A server can never ask the user anything; all input must arrive as tool arguments
A server can ask at any time as long as the client declared the elicitation capability

questions.explanation: Elicitation happens inside the handling of a request the client made, and the client mediates it: it may present, decline or cancel the prompt. Servers have no channel for spontaneously interrupting the user.

questions.question: How are MCP's security principles enforced?

options.text: By the protocol: a server cannot execute a tool until the client sends a consent token
By the registry: servers that fail a consent conformance test cannot be published
Not at the protocol level: implementors SHOULD build consent and access controls
By the host runtime: MCP SDKs refuse tool calls that lack a recorded user approval

questions.explanation: The specification states plainly that MCP itself cannot enforce these principles at the protocol level, and lists implementation guidelines that implementors SHOULD follow. There is no consent token in the wire protocol.

questions.question: What is true of every MCP extension, such as Tasks or MCP Apps?

options.text: It is negotiated once per connection, like capabilities were before 2026-07-28
It becomes mandatory for conformance one revision after it reaches Final
It is enabled by default once the SDK version supports it, and can be switched off
It is disabled by default and needs explicit support declared by both client and server

questions.explanation: Extensions are always opt-in and disabled by default. Clients advertise them in clientCapabilities.extensions on each request and servers in their server/discover capabilities; if only one side supports one, the supporting side falls back to core behaviour.

questions.question: Two implementations disagree about a message shape. Which artifact is the authoritative source of truth?

options.text: The official SDK implementations, which define the behaviour in practice
The prose specification pages, since the schema is only a convenience generated for tooling authors
The JSON Schema file, from which the TypeScript definitions are generated
The TypeScript schema (schema.ts) for the revision, from which the JSON Schema is generated

questions.explanation: The specification states that the protocol is defined by the TypeScript schema, which is the source of truth for all protocol messages and structures; the JSON Schema is generated from it automatically.
